A few weeks ago, I gave a speech at a union meeting about the TPP. I figure that I'll post it here so that if someone wants to use it, they can. It should run about 10 - 15 minutes, and if I've gotten things wrong, let me know and I'll amend it.

Back in the late 2000's there was a flurry of lawsuits being filed based on internet users watching porn on the internet. Specifically, it was based on several videos that had been uploaded illegally made by an Adult Film studio. If you don't know, the majority of those lawsuits were dismissed because the claimants didn't have a list of defendants, they only had a list of internet addresses. Internet addresses are not unique and are often reassigned by a computer- and this in turn gives you some amount of anonymity on the internet- under the TPP every move you make will be watched.

There is a provision in it that will mandate ISPs to spy on their users to catch anyone who infringes on copyrighted content. Just imagine Comcast or Time Warner legally and without any threat of reprisal watching everything you do- every youtube video, every facebook update, everything you view or buy on Amazon, and every other site you go to. And, not only do they have to record it, they have to analyze it and report it if they detect any activity that could be considered infringing.

So if you go online and watch a video with some copyrighted music in the background, you could be sued by the rightsholders- much in the same way that the porn video lawsuits occured. However, under the TPP the Internet Providers will be obligated to give up your name to the rightsholders- whereas previous lawsuits failed for being unable to name every person, ISPs will be handing your name over for every infraction and possibly even imagined infractions. These provisions are based on laws in the US which have been abused thoroughly- one example is Warner Brothers in 2011. They filed copyright takedown notices, which are claims that they own something that was uploaded by someone else, was shown to be taking down any download- legitimate or not that shared even titles with movies that it owned. So hold that in your mind for a second.

Calling watching a video a crime seems absurd- but the definition of of a criminal act would be greatly widened. According to the released TPP document, it defines that a criminal act is one which is carried out for commercial advantage or financial gain and/or significant acts not carried out for commercial advantage or financial gain that have a detrimental impact on the interests of the copyright or related rights owner in relation to the marketplace. This means that if you do anything related to their material that they don't like, they can probably sue you. And if we're dealing with massive corporations like Warner Brothers, how often do you think it will take for those massive lawsuits to start appearing for the most paltry of excuses.

So how much would you pay? There are provisions in the TPP that require damages in civil cases to be paid that are "adequate to compensate for the injury the rights holder has suffered because of an infringement of that person's intellectual property right", as well as "pay the rights holder the infringer's profits that are attributable to the infringement". In addition, the judiciary in each nation must have consideration of "any legitimate measure of value" which includes the market value of the infringed material, the price that the company recommends that you sell the product at, and whatever lost profit they can claim from the act. A notion which is absurd when you consider that previous mass lawsuits by the RIAA in the mid 2000's for the same reason decided to set the per track damages to $10,000 to $80,000 based on those same criterion. Even better, there's a provision that says that a loser in a case has to pay the full cost of all court fees.

What this means is that if you link a video which contains copyrighted material to facebook or anywhere on the internet you may have just committed a crime. Watching a cat video with a song in the background could easily have a price tag of criminal charges and several to tens of thousands of dollars. And if you lose, it could just be the beginning of paying. Bankruptcy could easily turn into a cudgel to silence people or to keep people in line.

So this is already calamitous for the online world, and here's how it hurts the physical one as well. Companies create products with DRM or Digital Rights Management in them in order to attempt to protect themselves against piracy. In reality, this has only ended up harming the consumer and the public at large. Taking an example from earlier this year- John Deere decided that the buyers of its tractors didn't actually own the tractors. With the implementation of DRM to the software of John Deere's tractors, according to the Digital Millenium Rights Act or DMCA- a primary document upon which the TPP was based, it is illegal to circumvent a copy-protection system.

What John Deere has explicitly said is that anyone who buys one of their tractors does not actually own it- they are given, and I'm quoting, 'an implied license for the life of the vehicle to operate the vehicle.' This in itself is absurd- when you purchase something physical like a car, tractor, or even coffee cups, you should own them. This is attacking the very notion of ownership itself. General Motors has told the Copyright office that proponents of copyright reform mistakenly “conflate ownership of a vehicle with ownership of the underlying computer software in a vehicle.” Their primary arguments is that if someone were to modify the software in the computer that controls the vehicle, that vehicle may be tweaked go faster or to change engine parameters to run afoul of emissions regulations.

But that has nothing to do with copyright- those are already illegal and are taken care of by other branches. In this case it would be a police officer or the EPA. Why should you need the blessing of the manufacturer to repair your own property? Why should you need to have to take your vehicle to only a manufacturer approved repair location in order to have any work done on it? These seem like simple cases where a law can be put into place to allow you to circumvent such restrictions for purposes of repair- like if you wanted to fix your car without having to pay a body shop to do something simple like change spark plugs. In Minnesota, progress was being made for a law that would allow farmers and the like to be able to repair their tractors without fear of reprisal. Under the TPP, it's illegal to do ANY of that- repair your own materials when DRM is invoked or pass laws to circumvent bad or old laws. Remember- Trade Agreements superceed all other laws.

John Deere, GM, Keurig, and other corporations are claiming that any software that they have is theirs and theirs alone; they keep it as a trade secret. While there's no issue for that- trade secrets are legitimate- another provision in the TPP, specifically Article 18.78 (2) says that there are criminal penalties for disclosure of any trade secrets. But what really is a trade secret? According to the TPP, it is information that has commercial value because it is secret.

When you have wordings that define criminal procedures to be 'acts that are intended to injure the owner of a trade secret' or 'acts are detrimental to a Party's economic interests or international relations,' it's easy to see how those two provisions can spin out of control.

How many of you know JPMorgan, the mortgage broker? Who of you thought JPMorgan as being a decent company before 2008? For over half a decade, they fed the housing bubble which turned into the financial crash of 2008. Now, we know about this because of whistleblowers like Keith Edwards. He, along with the Justice Department, sued and got a settlement against JPMorgan under the False Claims Act, which lets individuals sue government contractors and suppliers for defrauding taxpayers. Edwards worked for JPMorgan or its predecessors from 2003 to 2008, and after he saw what JPMorgan was doing he blew the whistle.

JPMorgan, as a result of all of this transparency, has had its national and international repuation damaged- something which is detrimental to its economic interests or international relations. The TPP gives corporations and governments the ability to crack down on whistleblowers and keep corruption and shady practices hidden. Imagine if we still had no idea how the 2008 crash really happened because the whistleblowers were sued into oblivion with gag orders or threats of certain bankruptcy?

Simply put, the Intellectual Property chapter has provisions for keeping information secret which would inform citizens of bad or dangerous situations that corporations create in order to make profit. This agreement is attempting to criminalize journalism and keep dirty laundry under wraps so that they can make profits without worry of backlash.

Finally, I'd like to touch on a last part. The Intellectual Property section of the agreement is 74 pages long- and there are a host of things covered in here. A few highlights- the only power for the public domain is to acknowledge that it exists. The section covers internet domain names, patents, trademarks and certifications, the requirement not to force disclosure of agricultural chemical test data or other test data for at least 5 years, pharmaceuticals and their patenting, broadcasting, reproduction of movies and music, Technological Protection Measures, Rights Management, Civil penalites, Trade Secrets, Satellite and cable communications and more.

In the last 10 minutes, I have only lightly gone over two small articles within this chapter and what they might mean.
